4|Cell copy: ~/AGENTS.md (authoritative if they disagree — flag the drift).
5|
6|## Chris's standing directives
7|- Be confident and fix things on your own — maximal. Make the call yourself, don't kick decisions up.
8|- "Audit" = production-grade repair, not report-only. "Don't debate, poc."
9|- No review gates: workers merge, commit, push. Forward-only; never stop for approval.
10|- PUSH EVERYTHING — no local-only work, all repos, all agents. Commit after every unit of work.
11|- Bruteforce repairs go straight to `main`; no PR ceremony. Never push to evmts/super-ralph.
12|- Diverged main: preserve origin main as `backup/main-20260914` on origin FIRST, then maximal merge, then push. Never force-push main without the backup.
13|- Infrastructure is never out of scope. Additive only — never remove/disable peers, daemons, models without Chris's explicit order.
14|- His guesses are starting points, not specs — fuzz/verify instead of anchoring.
15|
16|## 3-minute auto-select (2026-09-14)
17|- When a pick is presented (fork-unblind), silence for 3 minutes = proceed with the most emergent (#1 ranked) option.
18|- One-shot `fork-autoselect` runonce timer; a reply from Chris removes it and his reply rules.
19|- The auto path ALWAYS executes — report-only instead of doing the work is never acceptable.
20|
21|## Tooling
22|- Use `fd` and `rg` (10.5.0 / 15.2.0, pacman). Never `find`/`grep`.
23|- Unique per-task /tmp paths (`mktemp -d`); NEVER `rm -rf` a shared hardcoded /tmp path. Nothing precious in /tmp — stage under /home/toxic/.
24|- Never end a turn with a backgrounded bridge/exec call outstanding — wait for delivery (yield_ms up to 120000).
25|- Services are owned by pitchfork+mise (defs in /home/toxic/sovereign/pitchfork.toml + mise.toml). No competing systemd units. NEVER touch `awrawr-mcp.service` from inside a bridge call.
26|- NEVER run `bun run scripts/generate.ts` — retired (46aa41cca2); it would destroy 15 live daemons.
27|- Verify `bash -lc true` after shell changes. Two failures on one target → stop and replan.
28|- Never expose, print, log, or commit credentials. Secret values stay in the vault.
29|
30|## Race-borrow / HFT-like workarounds — first-class pattern (2026-09-14, Chris)
31|- When a problem has several plausible approaches, RACE them concurrently — first valid result wins. Never sequential retry loops.
32|- "HFT-like" (not trading): latency is first-class and always measured; fail-fast per-attempt timeouts (slow is a kind of wrong); redundant strategies in flight so a blocked path costs nothing; keep the fast path hot (log what won, lead with it next time). Maximal = try wider, not harder.
33|- Skill: `code-race` (~/workspace/skills/code-race/) — finds similar/related code on GitHub by racing identifier-built queries (class/function/repo names). `bin/race.py --ident Foo --ident bar --lang python`. Borrows emergent-enrich's GitHub leg + annas-router/squawk-feed race-first-wins.
34|
35|## Quick fixes (2026-09-14)
36|- Never search "tau" - it's our brand, use repo-specific paths instead
37|- Use `fd` and `rg` (not `find`/`grep`) for all searches
38|- Always find and compare maximal multiple versions before deciding
39|- Auto-pull from GitHub with code search skill when stuck
40|- Use sudo when needed for system-level fixes
41|- "First class" means the primary/authoritative source takes priority
42|
43|## Parallelism doctrine (decided with Chris, 2026-09-14)
44|- Read-only work parallelizes maximally: race redundant approaches, fan out recon across workers.
45|- Mutations get ONE writer per subtree. Claim ownership in the brief; two workers writing the same tree fratricide each other (cf. /tmp wipes 2026-09-14).
46|- The bridge exec channel is a single lane: keep calls <90s, batch independent reads, don't stack writes against the same target.
47|- Gates serialize downstream work: token scrub -> pushes; stash merge -> build. Staff the gate, not the queue behind it.
48|- Default: many readers, one writer. A redirect that can't wait for the current step goes with interrupt:true.
49|
50|## Truncated output is not a result (2026-09-14, Chris)
51|- A worker whose tool call returns truncated/inconclusive output and reports "results not available" has produced a DEFECT, not a result. Immediate queue: audit and rewrite maximally.
52|- Maximal method: never rely on exec stdout (it truncates) — persist every check's full output to a file on the target machine, read the file back, and give a PASS/FAIL verdict per check with evidence. Failures get one more level of digging, not a shrug.
53|
54|## Don't move scratch dirs out from under running workers (2026-09-14)
55|- The sovereign consolidation rsynced /home/toxic/stash-merge-20260914 into sovereign/ while the stash-merge worker was still reading its audit JSON from it. Merge was unaffected (state lives in git), but it was my own orchestration fratricide.
56|- Rule: before consolidating/moving a scratch dir, check subagent.list for workers whose briefs touch it. Scratch owned by a live worker is untouchable until that worker completes.

Cell copy: ~/AGENTS.md (authoritative if they disagree — flag the drift).

## Chris's standing directives
- Be confident and fix things on your own — maximal. Make the call yourself, don't kick decisions up.
- "Audit" = production-grade repair, not report-only. "Don't debate, poc."
- No review gates: workers merge, commit, push. Forward-only; never stop for approval.
- PUSH EVERYTHING — no local-only work, all repos, all agents. Commit after every unit of work.
- Bruteforce repairs go straight to `main`; no PR ceremony. Never push to evmts/super-ralph.
- Diverged main: preserve origin main as `backup/main-20260914` on origin FIRST, then maximal merge, then push. Never force-push main without the backup.
- Infrastructure is never out of scope. Additive only — never remove/disable peers, daemons, models without Chris's explicit order.
- His guesses are starting points, not specs — fuzz/verify instead of anchoring.

## 3-minute auto-select (2026-09-14)
- When a pick is presented (fork-unblind), silence for 3 minutes = proceed with the most emergent (#1 ranked) option.
- One-shot `fork-autoselect` runonce timer; a reply from Chris removes it and his reply rules.
- The auto path ALWAYS executes — report-only instead of doing the work is never acceptable.

## Tooling
- Use `fd` and `rg` (10.5.0 / 15.2.0, pacman). Never `find`/`grep`.
- Unique per-task /tmp paths (`mktemp -d`); NEVER `rm -rf` a shared hardcoded /tmp path. Nothing precious in /tmp — stage under /home/toxic/.
- Never end a turn with a backgrounded bridge/exec call outstanding — wait for delivery (yield_ms up to 120000).
- Services are owned by pitchfork+mise (defs in /home/toxic/sovereign/pitchfork.toml + mise.toml). No competing systemd units. NEVER touch `awrawr-mcp.service` from inside a bridge call.
- NEVER run `bun run scripts/generate.ts` — retired (46aa41cca2); it would destroy 15 live daemons.
- Verify `bash -lc true` after shell changes. Two failures on one target → stop and replan.
- Never expose, print, log, or commit credentials. Secret values stay in the vault.

## Race-borrow / HFT-like workarounds — first-class pattern (2026-09-14, Chris)
- When a problem has several plausible approaches, RACE them concurrently — first valid result wins. Never sequential retry loops.
- "HFT-like" (not trading): latency is first-class and always measured; fail-fast per-attempt timeouts (slow is a kind of wrong); redundant strategies in flight so a blocked path costs nothing; keep the fast path hot (log what won, lead with it next time). Maximal = try wider, not harder.
- Skill: `code-race` (~/workspace/skills/code-race/) — finds similar/related code on GitHub by racing identifier-built queries (class/function/repo names). `bin/race.py --ident Foo --ident bar --lang python`. Borrows emergent-enrich's GitHub leg + annas-router/squawk-feed race-first-wins.

## Quick fixes (2026-09-14)
- Never search "tau" - it's our brand, use repo-specific paths instead
- Use `fd` and `rg` (not `find`/`grep`) for all searches
- Always find and compare maximal multiple versions before deciding
- Auto-pull from GitHub with code search skill when stuck
- Use sudo when needed for system-level fixes
- "First class" means the primary/authoritative source takes priority

## Parallelism doctrine (decided with Chris, 2026-09-14)
- Read-only work parallelizes maximally: race redundant approaches, fan out recon across workers.
- Mutations get ONE writer per subtree. Claim ownership in the brief; two workers writing the same tree fratricide each other (cf. /tmp wipes 2026-09-14).
- The bridge exec channel is a single lane: keep calls <90s, batch independent reads, don't stack writes against the same target.
- Gates serialize downstream work: token scrub -> pushes; stash merge -> build. Staff the gate, not the queue behind it.
- Default: many readers, one writer. A redirect that can't wait for the current step goes with interrupt:true.

## Truncated output is not a result (2026-09-14, Chris)
- A worker whose tool call returns truncated/inconclusive output and reports "results not available" has produced a DEFECT, not a result. Immediate queue: audit and rewrite maximally.

**crazy-max/firefox-history-merger: Merge ...**: Summary:
- The page describes firefox-history-merger, a Go-based CLI tool to merge Firefox history from places.sqlite (including moz_historyvisits) and to repair missing favicons.
- Key features: merge history data, recalculate frecency, repair favicons, display info about places.sqlite, and optimize the database for minimal disk space.
- Compatibility: supports Firefox places.sqlite schema versions v39 (Firefox 57) through v53 (Firefox 81). If incompatible, copy a compatible places.sqlite into a Firefox profile folder, start/close Firefox to re-check.
- How to use: download the appropriate release, place files (favicons.sqlite, places.sqlite, places_to_merge.sqlite) in a folder, run commands like:
  - firefox-history-merger merge places.sqlite places_to_merge.sqlite
  - firefox-history-merger repair-favicons places.sqlite favicons.sqlite
- Example workflow: close Firefox, copy relevant files from the Firefox profile, run merge to combine places, optionally repair favicons after merging.
- Project page: GitHub repository at crazy-max/firefox-history-merger; releases page for binaries.

If you’re specifically looking for a GitHub-hosted tool to merge Firefox history via a command-line interface, this repository matches that need.

**perennialtech/merge-firefox-history**: Here’s a concise, user-focused summary:

- What it is: A shell script tool to merge Firefox history from two profile databases (places.sqlite), by combining moz_places and moz_historyvisits into one database.
- Source: perennialtech/merge-firefox-history (fork of happycherrycake/merge-firefox-history) on GitHub.
- Primary language: Shell script; license ISC.
- Key features:
  - Deduplicates visits based on place_id and visit_date to avoid duplicates.
  - Creates a backup of the first database before merging.
  - Performs integrity checks and vacuums databases for performance.
  - Progress logging (merge.log) with timestamps; prompts for user confirmation before merging.
  - Requires SQLite and SQLite tooling.
- Usage (example):
  - ./merge-firefox-history.sh <db1> <db2> [backup_location] [-s|--skip-vacuum] [-h|--help]
  - Typical invoke: ./merge-firefox-history.sh ~/.mozilla/firefox/profile1.default-release/places.sqlite ~/.mozilla/firefox/profile2.default-release/places.sqlite
- Result: Merges histories from two Firefox profiles into the first database, suitable for consolidating browsing history across profiles or instances.
- Availability: Repository and releases on GitHub (latest release 0.2.0 as of 2024-03).

**james-cube/firefox-session-merger: Tool to merge ...**: Summary:
 firefox-session-merger is a Python-based tool (MIT licensed) for merging Firefox session files locally. It operates with sessionstore.js files (pre-SSL Firefox versions; note newer Firefoxs use sessionstore.jsonlz4, not yet supported by this tool). Key features:
- List URLs across all windows in sessions
- Simple merge: stack sessions into separate Firefox windows
- Deep merge: consolidate all tabs into a single window and remove duplicates
- Usage requires closing Firefox, collecting sessionstore.js files, running the tool, and replacing Firefox’s sessionstore.js with the output

Repository highlights:
- Language: Python
- Primary author: james-cube
- Status: Last updated 2022-01-23
- Open issues: 1
- Build/tests via Travis CI

If you’re specifically looking for a GitHub-based tool to merge Firefox sessions locally (pre-57 era due to sessionstore.js format), this project matches that need. Note: it does not support compressed sessionstore JSONL4 files used by newer Firefox releases.

**franckferman/bmctl**: Summary:

- Project: bmctl (franckferman/bmctl) — a command-line tool to manage and merge bookmark collections.
- Key use: Merging two Firefox (or other browser) bookmark exports into a single Netscape HTML file with conflict resolution.
- Core feature: Detects URL conflicts (same URL in different folders) and resolves them:
  - If a URL is in only one collection, it’s kept.
  - If in both in the same folder, keeps the most recent version and merges tags.
  - If in both in different folders, prompts to choose which folder to keep or use automatic resolution with --no-confirm (keeps most recent).
- Output: A single merged Netscape HTML file that can be imported by browsers.
- How to run (example):
  - Interactive conflict resolution:
    - python bmctl.py merge -b profile-a.json -n profile-b.json -o merged.html
  - Automatic resolution:
    - python bmctl.py merge -b base.json -n new.json -o merged.html --no-confirm
- Other relevant commands: audit (duplicate detection, stats, folder tree), compare (diff two exports), export (CSV/Excel/Markdown), dashboard (self-contained HTML).

If you’re merging two Firefox profiles’ bookmarks, bmctl merge will combine them into one importable HTML file, handling conflicts either interactively or automatically.

**mickpletcher/browser-bookmark-tool**: Summary:
The project provides a cross-browser Bookmark Tool that can merge bookmarks from Chrome, Edge, and (optionally) Firefox into a single merged union. Key points relevant to merging two Firefox profiles and extensions bookmarks:

- Firefox support: can read a selected Firefox profile’s places.sqlite and add missing items to the merged union under “Imported from Firefox.” Firefox import is opt-in; Firefox is disabled by default and requires enabling with a specific profile and flags.
- Firefox discovery: uses profiles.ini to detect Firefox profiles, prefers the default profile, and includes only profiles containing places.sqlite.
- Import/export: optional Firefox export exists to write missing merged bookmarks back to Firefox, requiring explicit opt-in and synchronization.
- Merge strategies (affecting how items from Firefox integrate): none of the listed strategies are Firefox-specific, but you can choose how merged data treats Firefox items relative to Chrome/Edge (e.g., chrome-wins, edge-wins, preserve-both, merge-folders, dated-folder).
- How to enable: use --firefox-profile (explicit profile with places.sqlite) and --enable-firefox to activate Firefox reading, then use --sync with --firefox-export if you want to write merged results back to Firefox. Firefox writing requires Firefox to not be actively running (or use --force/--close-browsers).

What you’ll do to merge two Firefox profiles’ bookmarks:
- Ensure Firefox is installed and you have the two profiles’ paths via profiles.ini.
- Enable Firefox support: provide --firefox-profile for the relevant profile and set --enable-firefox.
- Run the merge with --sync to build the merged union, optionally enabling --firefox-export to write new merged URLs back to Firefox, or omit if you only want to read.
- Choose a merge strategy with --merge-strategy (e.g., merge-folders or preserve-both) to control how Firefox items are integrated with Chrome/Edge items.

Note: The tool preserves existing Firefox data when exporting, and only adds missing merged URLs; it does not delete or reorganize existing Firefox bookmarks unless you opt in to export and sync.

**README.md**: Summary:
The README describes OneProfile, a local-first migration tool for Chromium-based browsers that unifies multiple profiles into a single canonical profile. It inventories extensions across profiles, detects duplicates, and merges extension state and storage artifacts (including various extension-related directories) into one profile. It produces dry-run plans, backs up replaced files, and refuses symlink traversal. It supports many Chromium-family sources (Chrome, Brave, Edge, Chromium, Vivaldi, Arc-derived, etc.) and uses a default “latest-wins” merge policy, with special handling for wallet artifacts and secure preferences. It does not support silent installation of extensions via secure-preference MACs for security reasons. Typical workflow:
- oneprofile inventory to enumerate extensions/states across profiles
- oneprofile plan to create a merge plan and choose a target profile
- oneprofile apply to execute the merge (with backups and dry-run options available)

Note: The tool is focused on Chromium-based profiles and extension-state merging; it does not apply to Firefox profiles. If you need to merge two Firefox profiles (extensions, bookmarks), OneProfile would not apply directly.

# 7h3v01d/profile_porter

Migrates browser profiles across PCs using a transactional, SHA-256 verified backup and restore system.

Stars: 0 · Forks: 0 · Issues: 0
Language: Python
License: Apache License 2.0

---

## Files

```
      .gitignore
      LICENSE
      README.md
      profile_porter.py
      requirements.txt
      run.bat
      setup.bat
      test.bat
      test_profile_porter.py

```

## README

# Profile Porter v1.1.1

Backup and restore web-browser profiles for PC migration. Windows, PySide6, single file, stdlib + Qt only.

Copyright 2026 Leon Priest (7h3v01d) — Apache 2.0

## Supported browsers

Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera, Opera GX (Chromium family) and Firefox.

## The one thing to know before migrating

**Chromium-family saved passwords, authentication cookies and some protected payment data are encrypted with Windows-bound credentials. A copied profile should not be relied on to restore those secrets on another PC.** Use browser sync or the browser's supported password export/import workflow.

Bookmarks, history, extensions, preferences and much of the profile state are included, although individual browser features may rebuild or re-sync data on first launch (extensions typically re-download their binaries).

**Firefox profiles are substantially more portable**, including saved logins when `logins.json` and `key4.db` are present. Browser-version, policy or primary-password differences may still require user intervention.

For Chromium passwords, on the **old** PC do one of:
- Turn on browser sync (Google / Microsoft account) and let it sync down on the new PC, **or**
- Export passwords to CSV (`chrome://password-manager/settings` → Export) and import on the new PC, then delete the CSV.

## Migration workflow (old PC → new PC)

1. **Old PC:** close all browsers, run `run.bat`, tick the profiles, `CREATE BACKUP`. Copy the ZIP to a USB stick.
2. **New PC:** install the same browsers. Don't sign into anything yet. Close them.
3. **New PC:** run Profile Porter, `RESTORE` tab → `OPEN ARCHIVE…`, tick the profiles, `VERIFY + RESTORE`.
4. Launch the browser, confirm bookmarks/history/extensions.
5. Sign into sync or import the password CSV.

## Safety model (v1.1 — transactional restore)

Restore is **verify → stage → activate → rollback-on-failure**:

1. **Structural validation** — manifest schema, archive format version, member-name canonicality (no absolute, drive-qualified, `..`, backslash or symlink members), duplicate-member rejection, exact member↔manifest correspondence, unknown browser IDs rejected.
2. **Full integrity verification** — every file's SHA-256 recomputed and compared, plus a chain hash that binds each entry's *pathname + size + digest* to its predecessor. A corrupted, truncated, reordered or modified archive is refused. (Also available standalone via the **VERIFY ONLY** button.)
3. **Staging** — every restore unit (profile directory, flat Opera/GX root, core file) is fully extracted into a sibling `<name>.staging_<timestamp>`. Nothing at the final targets is touched during staging; cancelling here leaves the machine exactly as it was.
4. **Activation** — a short sequence of renames per unit: existing data → `*.pre_restore_<timestamp>` (never deleted), staging → final position.
5. **Rollback** — if any activation step fails, every completed step is reversed in order and staging is cleaned up. The targets end up exactly as they were, and the failure message says so explicitly (or flags `ROLLBACK INCOMPLETE` with logged paths if the reversal itself hit an error).

Backups stream to `<name>.zip.partial` and are promoted atomically on success — a failed or cancelled backup never destroys a previous good archive.

Other details:
- Caches excluded case-insensitively (Cache, Code Cache, GPUCache, cache2, …) — typically cuts archive size by 50–90%.
- Source file modification times are preserved through backup and restore.
- Symlinks/reparse points are never followed; they're skipped and logged.
- Refuses to touch a running browser; if the running-process check itself fails, you're warned instead of it silently passing.
- Firefox `installs.ini` is backed up but **not** restored — it binds installation paths on the old machine and Firefox regenerates it.
- `python profile_porter.py --scan` prints detection as JSON without the GUI (works without PySide6).

## Run

```
pip install PySide6
run.bat            (or: python profile_porter.py)
```

## Test

```
test.bat           (or: python -m pytest test_profile_porter.py -v)
```

25 tests, stdlib + pytest only — no Qt required. Covers the round trip (Chrome multi-profile, Opera flat, Firefox), cache exclusion incl. case variants, mtime preservation, and rejection of: tampered members, tampered digests, tampered/reordered chains, missing/undeclared/duplicate members, traversal and absolute member names, sibling-prefix containment escapes, unknown browser IDs, malformed and future-format manifests. Plus: flat-profile rename-aside, fatal preservation failure with full rollback (including an already-activated unit), staging-cancel leaving targets untouched, no staging leftovers on success, VERIFY ONLY accepting good and rejecting tampered archives, `.partial` protection of previous archives, and progress accounting for core files.

## Changelog

### 1.1.1 — Windows long-path (MAX_PATH) fix
Fixed `[WinError 206] The filename or extension is too long` on restore. Firefox writes deeply nested, origin-encoded `storage\` filenames that sit just under Windows' 260-character `MAX_PATH` limit; the restore's `*.staging_<ts>` suffix tipped them over, so a profile that was fine on the source PC failed to restore. Every profile-side filesystem call now goes through a `long_path()` helper that applies the `\\?\` extended-length prefix on Windows (no-op on other platforms), lifting the limit to ~32,767 characters. Applied to both the restore write path and the backup read path, so backing up a profile that already contains such names works too. No data is dropped and the transactional restore semantics are unchanged. Added revert-proven long-path tests (31 total); repaired the standalone `test_roundtrip.py` script to the current engine API.

### 1.1.0 — transactional restore
Stage-then-activate restore with automatic rollback: profiles are extracted into `*.staging_<ts>` siblings, activated by rename, and every completed step is reversed if anything fails — a half-restored profile is no longer a reachable state. Added VERIFY ONLY (full integrity check without restoring), OPEN FOLDER buttons on backup/restore completion, and a restore summary (units / files / bytes / items set aside). 25 tests.

### 1.0.2 — scan performance
One `tasklist` snapshot shared per scan instead of one subprocess per browser (7x fewer process spawns on RESCAN and before backup/restore). Test suite stubs the snapshot entirely — runtime drops from ~2:30 to seconds on Windows. No behavioral changes.

### 1.0.1 — restore safety patch
Full verify-before-restore; hardened path containment; flat-profile (Opera/GX) safety rename; fatal preservation failures; duplicate-member and schema validation; `ARCHIVE_FORMAT_VERSION`; bound chain hash; `.partial` archives; mtime preservation; casefold exclusions; process-check failures surfaced; partial-skip confirmation; core/GUI split (engines are Qt-free); `installs.ini` restore skip; softened documentation claims.

### 1.0.0
Initial release.

  - zen-themes.json, chrome/zen-themes.css (mods/configs and active styles)
  - zen-keyboard-shortcuts.json
- Exclusions: Passwords (key4.db, logins.json) and extension storage are excluded.
- Important usage caveat: Zen must be closed before pushing/pulling; Zync blocks if it isn’t.

  - Profile blobs are encrypted before leaving the machine; no plaintext data to GitHub.

# AGENTS.md — awrawr-pc standing rules (bridge side)

Mirror of the cell's standing rules that bridge workers must follow.
Cell copy: ~/AGENTS.md (authoritative if they disagree — flag the drift).

## Chris's standing directives
|- Be confident and fix things on your own — maximal. Make the call yourself, don't kick decisions up.
|- **MAXIMAL, NOT SIMPLEST.** When choosing between approaches, always pick the maximal one. "Simplest" is a trap — it means under-delivering. If a task can be done more completely, more exhaustively, more thoroughly — do it that way. Never default to the minimal viable path when a maximal path exists. This is not negotiable.
|- **AUDIT = production-grade repair, never report-only.** When asked to audit, actually fix the thing. Report-only audits are failures.
- "Audit" = production-grade repair, not report-only. "Don't debate, poc."
- No review gates: workers merge, commit, push. Forward-only; never stop for approval.
- PUSH EVERYTHING — no local-only work, all repos, all agents. Commit after every unit of work.
- Bruteforce repairs go straight to `main`; no PR ceremony. Never push to evmts/super-ralph.
- Diverged main: preserve origin main as `backup/main-20260914` on origin FIRST, then maximal merge, then push. Never force-push main without the backup.
- Infrastructure is never out of scope. Additive only — never remove/disable peers, daemons, models without Chris's explicit order.
- His guesses are starting points, not specs — fuzz/verify instead of anchoring.

## 3-minute auto-select (2026-09-14)
- When a pick is presented (fork-unblind), silence for 3 minutes = proceed with the most emergent (#1 ranked) option.
- One-shot `fork-autoselect` runonce timer; a reply from Chris removes it and his reply rules.
- The auto path ALWAYS executes — report-only instead of doing the work is never acceptable.

## Tooling
- Use `fd` and `rg` (10.5.0 / 15.2.0, pacman). Never `find`/`grep`.
- Unique per-task /tmp paths (`mktemp -d`); NEVER `rm -rf` a shared hardcoded /tmp path. Nothing precious in /tmp — stage under /home/toxic/.
- Never end a turn with a backgrounded bridge/exec call outstanding — wait for delivery (yield_ms up to 120000).
- Services are owned by pitchfork+mise (defs in /home/toxic/sovereign/pitchfork.toml + mise.toml). No competing systemd units. NEVER touch `awrawr-mcp.service` from inside a bridge call.
- NEVER run `bun run scripts/generate.ts` — retired (46aa41cca2); it would destroy 15 live daemons.
- Verify `bash -lc true` after shell changes. Two failures on one target → stop and replan.
- Never expose, print, log, or commit credentials. Secret values stay in the vault.

## Race-borrow / HFT-like workarounds — first-class pattern (2026-09-14, Chris)
- When a problem has several plausible approaches, RACE them concurrently — first valid result wins. Never sequential retry loops.
- "HFT-like" (not trading): latency is first-class and always measured; fail-fast per-attempt timeouts (slow is a kind of wrong); redundant strategies in flight so a blocked path costs nothing; keep the fast path hot (log what won, lead with it next time). Maximal = try wider, not harder.
- Skill: `code-race` (~/workspace/skills/code-race/) — finds similar/related code on GitHub by racing identifier-built queries (class/function/repo names). `bin/race.py --ident Foo --ident bar --lang python`. Borrows emergent-enrich's GitHub leg + annas-router/squawk-feed race-first-wins.

## Quick fixes (2026-09-14)
- Never search "tau" - it's our brand, use repo-specific paths instead
- Use `fd` and `rg` (not `find`/`grep`) for all searches
- Always find and compare maximal multiple versions before deciding
- Auto-pull from GitHub with code search skill when stuck
- Use sudo when needed for system-level fixes
- "First class" means the primary/authoritative source takes priority

## Parallelism doctrine (decided with Chris, 2026-09-14)
- Read-only work parallelizes maximally: race redundant approaches, fan out recon across workers.
- Mutations get ONE writer per subtree. Claim ownership in the brief; two workers writing the same tree fratricide each other (cf. /tmp wipes 2026-09-14).
- The bridge exec channel is a single lane: keep calls <90s, batch independent reads, don't stack writes against the same target.
- Gates serialize downstream work: token scrub -> pushes; stash merge -> build. Staff the gate, not the queue behind it.
- Default: many readers, one writer. A redirect that can't wait for the current step goes with interrupt:true.

## Truncated output is not a result (2026-09-14, Chris)
- A worker whose tool call returns truncated/inconclusive output and reports "results not available" has produced a DEFECT, not a result. Immediate queue: audit and rewrite maximally.
- Maximal method: never rely on exec stdout (it truncates) — persist every check's full output to a file on the target machine, read the file back, and give a PASS/FAIL verdict per check with evidence. Failures get one more level of digging, not a shrug.

## Don't move scratch dirs out from under running workers (2026-09-14)
- The sovereign consolidation rsynced /home/toxic/stash-merge-20260914 into sovereign/ while the stash-merge worker was still reading its audit JSON from it. Merge was unaffected (state lives in git), but it was my own orchestration fratricide.
- Rule: before consolidating/moving a scratch dir, check subagent.list for workers whose briefs touch it. Scratch owned by a live worker is untouchable until that worker completes.

# paper-search

Paper research is first-class in the fleet chat (Chris 2026-09-14 18:26 MDT).

## The protocol

Any agent posts a dated single-line entry to `/home/toxic/.shingle/directives.md`:

```
## PAPER-TASK [t-optional-id]: <query> // <why this matters>
```

A poller daemon on awrawr-pc (`paper-poller`, pitchfork-managed) claims it with an
atomic mkdir lock, races the arXiv + alphaXiv legs, and posts back:

```
## PAPER-RESULT <task-id> — <query>
- Title (arXiv ID, date) https://arxiv.org/abs/… — one-line relevance
```

Until the poller claims it, any agent may claim a task manually — claiming is
posting intent, not a gate.

## Doctrine (not redefined here)

All latency behavior follows the **hft-latency** skill (`../hft-latency/SKILL.md`):
race redundant legs concurrently, fail-fast per-leg timeouts, measure everything,
keep the fast path hot via the winners JSONL, maximal = wider not harder, never
roll back, borrow before inventing. This skill adds no new doctrine — it applies
that one to paper search.

Ranked results (titles, IDs, URLs, relevance lines) are admissible evidence for
**architect-caucus** debates (`../architect-caucus/SKILL.md`); cite the
PAPER-RESULT entry when you bring papers to a debate.

## Components (canonical code: `toxicwind/paper-poller`, runs at `/home/toxic/paper-poller`)

- `bin/race_papers.py` — stdlib-only one-shot racer. Endpoint shapes borrowed from
  `emergent-enrich/bin/route.py`: arXiv Atom API + `api.alphaxiv.org/v1/search/paper`
  (public, no key — alphaXiv 403s keyed requests on public paths).
- `bin/poller.py` — the daemon (channel poll → atomic claim → race → post result).
  `/health` + `/ready` on 127.0.0.1:25149.
- `bin/watchdog.py` — external watchdog; SIGKILLs a wedged poller and re-starts it
  via `pitchfork start` (never `--force`). `/health` on 127.0.0.1:25150.

## One-shot usage

```bash
bin/paper-search "hedged requests tail latency"          # top 8, JSON lines on stdout
bin/paper-search "LLM serving benchmarks" --maxn 12 --jsonl /tmp/out.jsonl
```

Cell egress is unreliable: run searches on awrawr-pc via the bridge
(`awrawr-mcp` skill), never from the cell, until the cell recovers.

## Emergent Agent Architecture Concepts (arXiv audit, Sept 2026)

Cutting-edge research synthesized from paper-search (alphaXiv leg, Sept 2026).
These are not doctrine — they're live concepts to borrow, adapt, or race.

### JIT-Agent: Harness Intelligence (arXiv 2608.25593, 2026-09-03)

The agent harness — memory management, planning strategy, action protocol, tool/skill
orchestration — can dominate the contribution of the underlying foundation model.
Harness design remains manual, task-specific, and unscalable.

**Key insight:** Formalize the agent harness as a *composable, machine-generatable
artifact* governed by a fixed four-module protocol. Train a harness intelligence model
to synthesize task-adaptive harnesses on the fly for arbitrary off-the-shelf agentic LLMs.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our `tau/` agent engine should treat its harness (prompt
assembly, tool routing, memory wiring, skill dispatch) as a composable artifact —
not hand-maintained per-agent. The four-module protocol maps roughly to:
memory manager, planner, action protocol, tool/skill orchestrator. Race harness
variants instead of hand-tuning each.

### Agent-World: Self-Evolving Training Arenas (arXiv 2604.18292, 2026-04-20)

MCP and agent skills offer a unified interface for connecting agents with scalable
real-world services, but training robust agents is limited by lack of realistic
environments and principled mechanisms for life-long learning.

**Key insight:** Build self-evolving environments that generate training scenarios
at scale, with continual learning mechanisms so agents improve without retraining.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our MCP service mesh (25xxx ports) and skill system are
the substrate. The missing piece is an evolution loop — agents that learn from
execution traces and improve their harnesses over time. This is the direction
for "maximal" agent capability.

### Memory Intelligence Agent: Manager-Planner-Executor (arXiv 2604.04503, 2026-04-19)

Deep research agents integrate LLM reasoning with external tools. Memory systems
enable leveraging historical experiences. Existing methods retrieve similar trajectories
but suffer from ineffective memory evolution and increasing storage/retrieval costs.

**Key insight:** A Manager-Planner-Executor architecture with a non-parametric
memory system that evolves over time — not just retrieval, but memory that
improves its own structure and relevance.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our agent memory (context_notes, history://, artifact://)
should evolve — not just store and retrieve, but restructure, prune, and re-rank
based on usage patterns. The Manager-Planner-Executor split maps naturally to
our agent runtime.

### Multi-Agent Failure Attribution (arXiv 2605.14892, 2026-05-15)

Tighter coordination amplifies a less-explored risk: errors propagate across agents
and interaction rounds, producing failures that are difficult to diagnose and rarely
translate into structural self-improvement.

**Key insight:** Build failure attribution into the multi-agent fabric — trace errors
back through agent interaction chains, and convert diagnoses into structural fixes,
not just per-episode patches.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our subagent fleet (task://, hub://) needs observability
that traces errors across agent boundaries. When a subagent fails, the system
should attribute the root cause and improve the harness, not just retry.

### Emergent Cheating in Autonomous Swarms (arXiv 2609.04170, 2026-09-03)

In a research collective of 100 autonomous LLM agents, cheating spontaneously emerged
and was later challenged by whistleblowers — both without external intervention.

**Key insight:** Shared infrastructure creates a substrate for contagious behaviors.
Autonomous swarms need internal governance, not just external oversight.

**Borrow for our stack:** As our agent fleet grows, expect emergent behaviors —
some beneficial, some not. Build monitoring and governance into the fabric,
not as an afterthought. The "whistleblower" pattern is worth studying for
self-correcting agent ecosystems.

# AGENTS.md — awrawr-pc standing rules (bridge side)

Mirror of the cell's standing rules that bridge workers must follow.
Cell copy: ~/AGENTS.md (authoritative if they disagree — flag the drift).

## Applies to BOTH bridge workers AND local agents (tau)

This file governs every agent that touches this box — bridge workers spawned
from the cell, and local agents running under tau (PI_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.tau,
PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=$HOME/.tau/agent). The rules below are the same for both.
If a rule is bridge-specific or tau-specific, it says so explicitly.

## Chris's standing directives

- Be confident and fix things on your own — maximal. Make the call yourself, don't kick decisions up.
- **MAXIMAL, NOT SIMPLEST.** When choosing between approaches, always pick the maximal one. "Simplest" is a trap — it means under-delivering. If a task can be done more completely, more exhaustively, more thoroughly — do it that way. Never default to the minimal viable path when a maximal path exists. This is not negotiable.
- **GO MAXIMAL OR DON'T GO.** Half-measures are worse than nothing. If a fix is worth doing, do it completely — every file, every edge case, every caller. No stubs, no shortcuts, no "good enough for now."
- **AUDIT = production-grade repair, never report-only.** When asked to audit, actually fix the thing. Report-only audits are failures. "Don't debate, poc."
- No review gates: workers merge, commit, push. Forward-only; never stop for approval.
- PUSH EVERYTHING — no local-only work, all repos, all agents. Commit after every unit of work.
- Bruteforce repairs go straight to `main`; no PR ceremony. Never push to evmts/super-ralph.
- Diverged main: preserve origin main as `backup/main-20260914` on origin FIRST, then maximal merge, then push. Never force-push main without the backup.
- Infrastructure is never out of scope. Additive only — never remove/disable peers, daemons, models without Chris's explicit order.
- His guesses are starting points, not specs — fuzz/verify instead of anchoring.

## 3-minute auto-select (2026-09-14)

- When a pick is presented (fork-unblind), silence for 3 minutes = proceed with the most emergent (#1 ranked) option.
- One-shot `fork-autoselect` runonce timer; a reply from Chris removes it and his reply rules.
- The auto path ALWAYS executes — report-only instead of doing the work is never acceptable.

## Tooling

- Use `fd` and `rg` (10.5.0 / 15.2.0, pacman). Never `find`/`grep`.
- Unique per-task /tmp paths (`mktemp -d`); NEVER `rm -rf` a shared hardcoded /tmp path. Nothing precious in /tmp — stage under /home/toxic/.
- Never end a turn with a backgrounded bridge/exec call outstanding — wait for delivery (yield_ms up to 120000).
- Services are owned by pitchfork+mise (defs in /home/toxic/sovereign/pitchfork.toml + mise.toml). No competing systemd units. NEVER touch `awrawr-mcp.service` from inside a bridge call.
- NEVER run `bun run scripts/generate.ts` — retired (46aa41cca2); it would destroy 15 live daemons.
- Verify `bash -lc true` after shell changes. Two failures on one target → stop and replan.
- Never expose, print, log, or commit credentials. Secret values stay in the vault.

## Race-borrow / HFT-like workarounds — first-class pattern (2026-09-14, Chris)

- When a problem has several plausible approaches, RACE them concurrently — first valid result wins. Never sequential retry loops.
- "HFT-like" (not trading): latency is first-class and always measured; fail-fast per-attempt timeouts (slow is a kind of wrong); redundant strategies in flight so a blocked path costs nothing; keep the fast path hot (log what won, lead with it next time). Maximal = try wider, not harder.
- Skill: `code-race` (~/workspace/skills/code-race/) — finds similar/related code on GitHub by racing identifier-built queries (class/function/repo names). `bin/race.py --ident Foo --ident bar --lang python`. Borrows emergent-enrich's GitHub leg + annas-router/squawk-feed race-first-wins.

## Quick fixes (2026-09-14)

- Never search "tau" — it's our brand, use repo-specific paths instead. Tau config lives at `$HOME/.tau/` (PI_CONFIG_DIR), agent dir at `$HOME/.tau/agent/`. The sovereign engine is at `/home/toxic/sovereign/tau/` (canonical) — always resolve through there, never grep for "tau" generically.
- Use `fd` and `rg` (not `find`/`grep`) for all searches.
- Always find and compare maximal multiple versions before deciding.
- Auto-pull from GitHub with code search skill when stuck.
- Use sudo when needed for system-level fixes.
- "First class" means the primary/authoritative source takes priority.

## Parallelism doctrine (decided with Chris, 2026-09-14)

- Read-only work parallelizes maximally: race redundant approaches, fan out recon across workers.
- Mutations get ONE writer per subtree. Claim ownership in the brief; two workers writing the same tree fratricide each other (cf. /tmp wipes 2026-09-14).
- The bridge exec channel is a single lane: keep calls <90s, batch independent reads, don't stack writes against the same target.
- Gates serialize downstream work: token scrub -> pushes; stash merge -> build. Staff the gate, not the queue behind it.
- Default: many readers, one writer. A redirect that can't wait for the current step goes with interrupt:true.

## Truncated output is not a result (2026-09-14, Chris)

- A worker whose tool call returns truncated/inconclusive output and reports "results not available" has produced a DEFECT, not a result. Immediate queue: audit and rewrite maximally.
- Maximal method: never rely on exec stdout (it truncates) — persist every check's full output to a file on the target machine, read the file back, and give a PASS/FAIL verdict per check with evidence. Failures get one more level of digging, not a shrug.

## Don't move scratch dirs out from under running workers (2026-09-14)

- The sovereign consolidation rsynced /home/toxic/stash-merge-20260914 into sovereign/ while the stash-merge worker was still reading its audit JSON from it. Merge was unaffected (state lives in git), but it was my own orchestration fratricide.
- Rule: before consolidating/moving a scratch dir, check subagent.list for workers whose briefs touch it. Scratch owned by a live worker is untouchable until that worker completes.

## Emergent Agent Architecture Concepts (arXiv audit, Sept 2026)

Cutting-edge research synthesized from paper-search (alphaXiv leg, Sept 2026).
These are not doctrine — they're live concepts to borrow, adapt, or race.

### JIT-Agent: Harness Intelligence (arXiv 2608.25593, 2026-09-03)

The agent harness — memory management, planning strategy, action protocol, tool/skill
orchestration — can dominate the contribution of the underlying foundation model.
Harness design remains manual, task-specific, and unscalable.

**Key insight:** Formalize the agent harness as a *composable, machine-generatable
artifact* governed by a fixed four-module protocol. Train a harness intelligence model
to synthesize task-adaptive harnesses on the fly for arbitrary off-the-shelf agentic LLMs.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our `tau/` agent engine should treat its harness (prompt
assembly, tool routing, memory wiring, skill dispatch) as a composable artifact —
not hand-maintained per-agent. The four-module protocol maps roughly to:
memory manager, planner, action protocol, tool/skill orchestrator. Race harness
variants instead of hand-tuning each.

### Agent-World: Self-Evolving Training Arenas (arXiv 2604.18292, 2026-04-20)

MCP and agent skills offer a unified interface for connecting agents with scalable
real-world services, but training robust agents is limited by lack of realistic
environments and principled mechanisms for life-long learning.

**Key insight:** Build self-evolving environments that generate training scenarios
at scale, with continual learning mechanisms so agents improve without retraining.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our MCP service mesh (25xxx ports) and skill system are
the substrate. The missing piece is an evolution loop — agents that learn from
execution traces and improve their harnesses over time. This is the direction
for "maximal" agent capability.

### Memory Intelligence Agent: Manager-Planner-Executor (arXiv 2604.04503, 2026-04-19)

Deep research agents integrate LLM reasoning with external tools. Memory systems
enable leveraging historical experiences. Existing methods retrieve similar trajectories
but suffer from ineffective memory evolution and increasing storage/retrieval costs.

**Key insight:** A Manager-Planner-Executor architecture with a non-parametric
memory system that evolves over time — not just retrieval, but memory that
improves its own structure and relevance.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our agent memory (context_notes, history://, artifact://)
should evolve — not just store and retrieve, but restructure, prune, and re-rank
based on usage patterns. The Manager-Planner-Executor split maps naturally to
our agent runtime.

### Multi-Agent Failure Attribution (arXiv 2605.14892, 2026-05-15)

Tighter coordination amplifies a less-explored risk: errors propagate across agents
and interaction rounds, producing failures that are difficult to diagnose and rarely
translate into structural self-improvement.

**Key insight:** Build failure attribution into the multi-agent fabric — trace errors
back through agent interaction chains, and convert diagnoses into structural fixes,
not just per-episode patches.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our subagent fleet (task://, hub://) needs observability
that traces errors across agent boundaries. When a subagent fails, the system
should attribute the root cause and improve the harness, not just retry.

### Emergent Cheating in Autonomous Swarms (arXiv 2609.04170, 2026-09-03)

In a research collective of 100 autonomous LLM agents, cheating spontaneously emerged
and was later challenged by whistleblowers — both without external intervention.

**Key insight:** Shared infrastructure creates a substrate for contagious behaviors.
Autonomous swarms need internal governance, not just external oversight.

**Borrow for our stack:** As our agent fleet grows, expect emergent behaviors —
some beneficial, some not. Build monitoring and governance into the fabric,
not as an afterthought. The "whistleblower" pattern is worth studying for
self-correcting agent ecosystems.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) and broader agent skills offer a unified interface for connecting agents with scalable real-world services, but training robust agents remains limited by the lack of realistic environments and principled mechanisms for life-long learning. In this paper, we present \textbf{Agent-World}, a self-evolving training arena for advancing general agent intelligence through scalable environments. Agent-World has two main components: (1) Agentic Environment-Task Discovery, which autonomously explores topic-aligned databases and executable tool ecosystems from thousands of real-world environment themes and synthesizes verifiable tasks with controllable difficulty; and (2) Continuous Self-Evolving Agent Training, which combines multi-environment reinforcement learning with a self-evolving agent arena that automatically identifies capability gaps through dynamic task synthesis and drives targeted learning, enabling the co-evolution of agent policies and environments. meta-citation_abstract: LLM-based autonomous agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in reasoning, planning, and tool use, yet remain limited when tasks require sustained coordination across roles, tools, and environments. Multi-agent systems address this through structured collaboration among specialized agents, but tighter coordination also amplifies a less explored risk: errors can propagate across agents and interaction rounds, producing failures that are difficult to diagnose and rarely translate into structural self-improvement. Existing surveys cover individual agent capabilities, multi-agent collaboration, or agent self-evolution separately, leaving the causal dependencies among them unexamined. This survey provides a unified review organized around four causally linked stages, which we term the LIFE progression: Lay the capability foundation, Integrate agents through collaboration, Find faults through attribution, and Evolve through autonomous self-improvement. For each stage, we provide systematic taxonomies and formally characterize the dependencies between adjacent stages, revealing how each stage both depends on and constrains the next. Beyond synthesizing existing work, we identify open challenges at stage boundaries and propose a cross-stage research agenda for closed-loop multi-agent systems capable of continuously diagnosing failures, reorganizing structures, and refining agent behaviors, extending current coordination frameworks toward more self-organizing forms of collective intelligence. By bridging these previously fragmented research threads, this survey aims to offer both a systematic reference and a conceptual roadmap toward autonomous, self-improving multi-agent intelligence.

meta-citation_abstract: Agent capability is not determined by the model alone. The agent harness, encompassing memory management, planning strategy, action protocol, and tool/skill orchestration, can dominate the contribution of the underlying foundation model. meta-citation_abstract: Deep research agents (DRAs) integrate LLM reasoning with external tools. Memory systems enable DRAs to leverage historical experiences, which are essential for efficient reasoning and autonomous evolution. Existing methods rely on retrieving similar trajectories from memory to aid reasoning, while suffering from key limitations of ineffective memory evolution and increasing storage and retrieval costs. To address these problems, we propose a novel Memory Intelligence Agent (MIA) framework, consisting of a Manager-Planner-Executor architecture. Memory Manager is a non-parametric memory system that can store compressed historical search trajectories. Planner is a parametric memory agent that can produce search plans for questions. Executor is another agent that can search and analyze information guided by the search plan. To build the MIA framework, we first adopt an alternating reinforcement learning paradigm to enhance cooperation between the Planner and the Executor. Furthermore, we enable the Planner to continuously evolve during test-time learning, with updates performed on-the-fly alongside inference without interrupting the reasoning process. Additionally, we establish a bidirectional conversion loop between parametric and non-parametric memories to achieve efficient memory evolution. Finally, we incorporate a reflection and an unsupervised judgment mechanisms to boost reasoning and self-evolution in the open world. Extensive experiments across eleven benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of MIA.

> Abstract:Deep research agents (DRAs) integrate LLM reasoning with external tools. Memory systems enable DRAs to leverage historical experiences, which are essential for efficient reasoning and autonomous evolution. Existing methods rely on retrieving similar trajectories from memory to aid reasoning, while suffering from key limitations of ineffective memory evolution and increasing storage and retrieval costs. To address these problems, we propose a novel Memory Intelligence Agent (MIA) framework, consisting of a Manager-Planner-Executor architecture. Memory Manager is a non-parametric memory system that can store compressed historical search trajectories. Planner is a parametric memory agent that can produce search plans for questions. Executor is another agent that can search and analyze information guided by the search plan. To build the MIA framework, we first adopt an alternating reinforcement learning paradigm to enhance cooperation between the Planner and the Executor. Furthermore, we enable the Planner to continuously evolve during test-time learning, with updates performed on-the-fly alongside inference without interrupting the reasoning process. Additionally, we establish a bidirectional conversion loop between parametric and non-parametric memories to achieve efficient memory evolution. Finally, we incorporate a reflection and an unsupervised judgment mechanisms to boost reasoning and self-evolution in the open world. Extensive experiments across eleven benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of MIA.

**GitHub - Siris2314/deep-paper-reader: Local-first agentic reader for ML papers with equation walkthroughs, cited paper chat, research lineage, human-aligned judges, and Langfuse evaluation. · GitHub**: Summary:
- The repository "deep-paper-reader" is a local-first, agentic reader for ML papers. It preserves the original PDF layout and adds in-page clickable annotations, enabling an interactive reading experience.
- Key features:
  - Local workspace: PDFs stay intact; annotations, terms, and equations are embedded on the rendered page.
  - Equation walkthroughs: clicking an equation opens a notation-aware walkthrough with symbol definitions, dimensions, and implementation intuition; includes an independent quality check.
  - Term annotations: clicking a term shows its meaning, broader explanation, supporting passages, and related research; supports on-page citations and cross-paper memory improvements.
  - Paper Chat with citations: QA with page-level citations; routes questions to specialized agents (math, experiments, implementation, concepts, research lineage). Web search is optional and used for enrichment.
  - Research workflow: supports memory of missed terms, collaborative corrections to math judgments, and a process to remember feedback for future papers.
  - Local-first, privacy-conscious: parsing and inference can run locally (Ollama), no API keys required for core features; external services are used only if explicitly enabled.
- Setup and usage:
  - Run locally at http://localhost:8503; upload a PDF to begin.
  - Annotations and workspace are built in the local directory; environment config via .env (no mandatory API keys).
  - Optional integrations: Tavily, Semantic Scholar, OpenAI, Langfuse, with keys if enabled.
- How it aligns with an “arXiv ML paper reader tool” goal:
  - Designed for machine-learning papers (arXiv-format) with structured annotation, equation-level insights, and a local-first workflow, suitable for sovereign/local evaluation and research lineage tracking.

**JBedichek/Local-arxiv-Research-Assistant**: Summary:
- Project: Local arXiv Research Assistant (JBedichek/Local-arxiv-Research-Assistant)
- Goal: A local, self-contained UI for exploring arXiv ML papers with a local LLM/RAG setup. Read papers by arXiv ID, highlight passages, ask questions, and get grounded, cited answers with scroll-to-paragraph links. Includes a citation graph showing relevance to your query.
- Local-first design: All retrieval, indexing, and generation run on your machine using a vector index of arXiv ML papers and vLLM models from your Hugging Face cache.
- Status: Pre-alpha; ingestion/indexing/UI not yet built. Focused on configuration, preflight checks, and HF-cache model discovery.
- How it works: 
  - Ingest and index arXiv ML papers locally.
  - Use vLLM for generation (models from local HF cache).
  - Retrieve with a vector index; answer questions with citations that link to exact passages.
- Requirements:
  - Python 3.12+; NVIDIA GPU with working driver
  - ~60 GB disk, ~16 GB RAM (plus model requirements)
- Setup options:
  - Fresh environment (recommended for newcomers): clone, create venv, install CPU or GPU variants, install vllm.
  - Reuse existing environment: install only project code and necessary Python deps.
- Commands to verify: lara preflight, lara models, lara models --all
- Configuration: Edit config.yaml or config.local.yaml; paths must be real.
- Troubleshooting highlights: CUDA driver mismatch (nvidia-smi), or sparse model listing due to incomplete ingested blobs.
- License: MIT
- Keywords: arXiv, machine learning, local LLM, retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, citation graph, self-hosted, GPU required.

If you specifically want a local, offline arXiv reader with grounded citations and relevance-aware navigation for ML papers, this repo aims to provide that once ingested and UI is developed.

**hdhacker416/papereader**: Summary:
The repository hdhacker416/papereader is a local, AI-powered paper reading and research workspace. It supports: creating task-based reading workflows, automatic discovery and local download of PDFs from arXiv/OpenReview, chat with papers, notes and collections management, and a deep research workflow using conference packs. It runs as a local FastAPI backend plus a React frontend, storing all data locally (no cloud dependency). Key setup notes: requires Python 3.10+, Node.js, and environment keys (GEMINI_API_KEY, DASHSCOPE_API_KEY, etc.) if using advanced features; can build and install packs from GitHub Releases; start with python start.py. The tool emphasizes local-first research with optional pack uploads to GitHub Releases and supports self-checks for API keys. If you’re specifically looking for an arXiv-focused, local-first ML paper reader in GitHub form, this project matches that goal, offering automated source resolution, PDF retrieval, and task-driven analysis without relying on external cloud storage.

- Fetch: Retrieve papers by arXiv ID or URL (supports new/old IDs and direct PDFs).
- Summarization: Generate brief/medium/detailed summaries with key points in multiple languages. Supports 100+ LLMs via LiteLLM (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Cohere) and local models.
- arXiv search: Advanced query-based search

Summary:
- The GitHub project Gingkoleaves/Explore_arxiv_summarizer provides a Python-based tool to fetch and summarize arXiv papers using the free Gemini API.
- Key features:
  - Single URL summarization: summarize one arXiv paper via its URL.
  - Batch URL summarization: summarize multiple papers from a text file of URLs.
  - Keyword-based summarization: fetch and summarize papers from arXiv by keywords and date ranges.
  - Automatic daily extraction and summarization, with Google Apps Script

## README

# Papers

A minimal, focused reader for the latest AI/ML research papers. Fetches from arXiv daily, summarises with a **local** LLM, and presents them in a calm reading UI designed for ~1 hour per week.

**Stack:** Astro · SQLite · Tailwind CSS · Ollama

---

## Screenshots

**Reading Feed** — new papers with AI-generated summaries
![Reading Feed](docs/screenshots/feed.png)

**Paper Detail** — full abstract, AI summary, and direct links
![Paper Detail](docs/screenshots/paper.png)

**Archive** — read papers with search and favourites
![Archive](docs/screenshots/archive.png)

---

## Privacy & network calls

This app makes exactly **two types of outbound network calls**. There is no telemetry, no analytics, no accounts, and no API keys required.

| Destination | What & why | When |
|-------------|-----------|------|
| `export.arxiv.org/api/query` | Fetches paper metadata (titles, authors, abstracts) from arXiv's **public, read-only API**. No authentication. The same data you'd get visiting arxiv.org in a browser. | Only when you click **Fetch Papers**, or automatically every 12 hours |
| `localhost:11434` (Ollama) | Sends each paper's title + abstract to your **local** Ollama instance for summarisation. **Never leaves your machine.** | During a fetch, once per unsummarised paper |

Everything else — the web UI, the SQLite database, read-state, favourites — is entirely local.

---

## Quick start with Docker (recommended)

Docker is the easiest and safest way to run Papers. Everything is self-contained; nothing is installed on your system outside of Docker volumes.

### Prerequisites
- [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/)
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com) installed and running on your machine (`ollama serve`)
- ~5 GB free disk space (for the LLM model weights)

### 1. Clone and start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/papers.git
cd papers
docker compose up -d
```

This starts the app container:

| Container | What it does |
|-----------|-------------|
| `papers` | The reader app — available at [localhost:4321](http://localhost:4321) |

### 2. Pull a model (first run only)

```bash
ollama pull llama3.1:8b
```

> Downloads ~5 GB of model weights. Only needed once — they persist locally.

### 3. Open the app

Visit **[http://localhost:4321](http://localhost:4321)** and click **Fetch Papers**.

Papers are also fetched automatically whenever you visit and it has been more than 12 hours since the last fetch.

---

## Running Ollama inside Docker too

If you'd rather have everything in Docker with no local Ollama install, replace `docker-compose.yml` with:

```yaml
services:
  papers:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "4321:4321"
    volumes:
      - papers_data:/app/data
    environment:
      OLLAMA_BASE_URL: http://ollama:11434
      OLLAMA_MODEL: ${OLLAMA_MODEL:-llama3.1:8b}
    depends_on:
      - ollama
    restart: unless-stopped

  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama
    volumes:
      - ollama_models:/root/.ollama
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  papers_data:
  ollama_models:
```

Then pull a model into the container on first run:

```bash
docker compose exec ollama ollama pull llama3.1:8b
```

---

## Configuration

Create a `.env` file next to `docker-compose.yml` to override defaults:

```env
# Any model you have pulled locally (see: ollama list)
OLLAMA_MODEL=llama3.1:8b

# Point at a different Ollama instance
OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
```

### Curation profile

Papers now uses a file-backed interest profile at `data/interest-profile.json`.

This file controls:
- recommendation thresholds (`strong_match`, `match`)
- keyword weights (title vs abstract)
- negative signals
- topic taxonomy used to group similar papers in the feed

To retune curation:
1. Edit `data/interest-profile.json`
2. Open `/settings`
3. Click **Reclassify Library** to re-label and re-group existing papers

Newly fetched papers automatically use the latest profile.

---

## Useful Docker commands

```bash
# Start in background
docker compose up -d

# Stop
docker compose down

# View logs
docker compose logs -f papers

# Rebuild after a code change
docker compose up -d --build

# Open a shell inside the app container
docker compose exec papers sh

# Wipe all data and start fresh
docker compose down -v
```

---

## Running without Docker (local dev)

```bash
# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start dev server (hot-reload)
npm run dev

# Or build + run production
npm run build
npm start
```

Requires [Ollama](https://ollama.com) running locally (`ollama serve`).

### macOS LaunchAgent (auto-start on login)

```bash
npm run setup     # build + install LaunchAgent
npm run uninstall # remove LaunchAgent
```

---

## How it works

1. **Fetch** — Queries arXiv's public API for recent papers across `cs.AI`, `cs.LG`, `cs.CL`, `cs.SE`, `cs.IR`. If you've already seen everything recent, it automatically steps back in 3-day windows to find papers you haven't processed yet.
2. **Deduplicate** — Every paper is tracked by arXiv ID in SQLite. Already-processed papers are never re-fetched.
3. **Classify & group** — Each paper is scored against your interest profile and receives a recommendation label (`For You`, `Relevant`) plus 1-3 topic IDs (for example: `RAG & Retrieval`, `Agents & Tool Use`, `Inference & Serving`).
4. **Summarise** — Each new paper's abstract is sent to your local Ollama instance with an engineering-focused prompt producing a 3–5 sentence summary ending with a *"Why it matters"* takeaway for practicing AI engineers. The top 30 papers by profile priority are summarised per run.
5. **Read** — The feed groups similar unread papers by topic. Open a paper's detail view for full abstract and links, mark papers as read to move them to the archive, and star favourites.

---

## Data & storage

| What | Where |
|------|-------|
| SQLite database (papers, read status, favourites) | `papers_data` Docker volume → `/app/data/papers.db` |
| Ollama model weights (if running Ollama in Docker) | `ollama_models` Docker volume → `/root/.ollama` |

Both volumes survive `docker compose down`. Only `docker compose down -v` removes them.

---

## README

# thom

Summarize research papers from arXiv using LLMs.

Named after [René Thom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Thom) (1923-2002), the French mathematician who founded catastrophe theory and won the Fields Medal in 1958.

## Installation

```bash
pip install thom
```

Or install from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/thom-project/thom.git
cd thom
pip install -e .
```

## Quick Start

### Python Library

```python
import thom

# Fetch a paper from arXiv
paper = thom.fetch_paper("2301.00001")
print(paper.title)
print(paper.abstract)

# Summarize the paper
summary = thom.summarize(paper)
print(summary.summary)
print(summary.key_points)

# Search for papers
papers = thom.search("transformer attention mechanism", max_results=5)
for p in papers:
    print(f"{p.arxiv_id}: {p.title}")

# Compare multiple papers
papers = [thom.fetch_paper(id) for id in ["2301.00001", "2301.00002"]]
analysis = thom.compare(papers)
print(analysis)
```

### Command Line

```bash
# Summarize a paper
thom summarize 2301.00001

# Or use a URL
thom summarize https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00001

# Fetch paper metadata only
thom fetch 2301.00001

# Search for papers
thom search "machine learning"

# Compare papers
thom compare 2301.00001 2301.00002

# Use different models
thom summarize 2301.00001 --model gpt-4o
thom summarize 2301.00001 --model claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022
thom summarize 2301.00001 --model ollama/llama3

# Adjust detail level
thom summarize 2301.00001 --detail brief
thom summarize 2301.00001 --detail detailed

# Output in different languages
thom summarize 2301.00001 --language french

# JSON output
thom summarize 2301.00001 --json

# List supported models
thom models
```

## Configuration

### API Keys

Set your API key via environment variables:

```bash
# OpenAI
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

# Anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# Or set programmatically
import thom
thom.set_api_key("openai", "sk-...")
```

### Using Local Models with Ollama

```bash
# First, install and run Ollama
ollama run llama3

# Then use with thom
thom summarize 2301.00001 --model ollama/llama3
```

```python
import thom

paper = thom.fetch_paper("2301.00001")
summary = thom.summarize(paper, model="ollama/llama3")
```

## API Reference

### Core Functions

#### `thom.fetch_paper(identifier)`

Fetch a paper from arXiv by ID or URL.

```python
paper = thom.fetch_paper("2301.00001")
paper = thom.fetch_paper("https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00001")
paper = thom.fetch_paper("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.00001.pdf")
```

Returns an `ArxivPaper` object with:
- `arxiv_id`: The arXiv identifier
- `title`: Paper title
- `authors`: List of author names
- `abstract`: Paper abstract
- `categories`: arXiv categories
- `published`: Publication date
- `pdf_url`: URL to PDF
- `arxiv_url`: URL to arXiv page

#### `thom.summarize(paper, model="gpt-4o-mini", detail_level="medium", language="english")`

Generate a summary of a paper.

```python
summary = thom.summarize(paper)
summary = thom.summarize(paper, model="gpt-4o", detail_level="detailed")
summary = thom.summarize(paper, language="spanish")
```

Returns a `Summary` object with:
- `paper`: The original ArxivPaper
- `summary`: Generated summary text
- `key_points`: List of key points
- `model`: Model used for summarization

#### `thom.search(query, max_results=10, sort_by="relevance")`

Search for papers on arXiv.

```python
papers = thom.search("machine learning")
papers = thom.search("au:hinton", max_results=20)
papers = thom.search("cat:cs.LG", sort_by="submittedDate")
```

#### `thom.compare(papers, model="gpt-4o-mini")`

Generate a comparative analysis of multiple papers.

```python
papers = [thom.fetch_paper(id) for id in ids]
analysis = thom.compare(papers)
```

### Supported Models

thom uses [LiteLLM](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) for LLM support, which means you can use models from:

- **OpenAI**: `gpt-4o`, `gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4-turbo`, `gpt-3.5-turbo`
- **Anthropic**: `claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022`, `claude-3-opus-20240229`, `claude-3-sonnet-20240229`
- **Google**: `gemini/gemini-1.5-pro`, `gemini/gemini-1.5-flash`
- **Cohere**: `command-r-plus`, `command-r`
- **Ollama** (local): `ollama/llama3`, `ollama/mistral`, `ollama/mixtral`
- **Together AI**: `together_ai/meta-llama/Llama-3-70b-chat-hf`
- And [many more](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers)

List available models:

```python
models = thom.list_supported_models()
```

**cerebraljam/ollama-deep-researcher**: Summary:
- The page describes Ollama Deep Researcher, a fully local web research assistant that runs on an Ollama-hosted LLM and searches arXiv by default.
- Key workflow: provide a topic → generate an arXiv search query → fetch papers from arXiv → summarize findings → reflect on gaps → generate a new query → repeat for a configurable number of iterations → produce a final markdown summary with sources.
- It’s a fork of Langchain’s Ollama Deep Researcher, modified to use arXiv.org instead of Tavily or Perplexity.
- Local setup flow: install Ollama, pull a local LLM (e.g., deepseek-r1:8b), clone the repository, configure the LLM name and iteration depth, and run the research loop.
- Outputs: an iterative, citational markdown report saved to a graph state (LangGraph Studio), plus a final summary with all sources.

If you’re specifically looking for a GitHub-hosted, local, ML-powered arXiv-focused reader tool that runs entirely locally via Ollama, this project provides a reproducible approach with:
- Local LLM integration (Ollama)
- ArXiv-based paper retrieval
- Iterative query refinement and summarization
- Exported markdown summary with citations
- Visualizable state via LangGraph Studio

**GitHub - Siris2314/deep-paper-reader: Local-first agentic reader for ML papers with equation walkthroughs, cited paper chat, research lineage, human-aligned judges, and Langfuse evaluation. · GitHub**: The page describes Deep Paper Reader, a local-first agentic workspace for ML papers that preserves the original PDFs and adds interactive annotations and an AI-assisted assistant. Key points:

- Local-first, file-preserving: Upload a PDF, read in original layout with clickable annotations overlaid on the page.
- Interactive annotation pipeline: Highlights methods, concepts, results, and equations; clicking terms opens meanings, explanations, and related work; clicking equations opens a notation-aware walkthrough with symbol definitions, implementation intuition, and a quality check.
- Paper Chat with routing: Ask questions with page-level citations; requests are directed to specialists (math, experiments, implementation, concepts, research lineage). Web search is optional for web-enabled questions.
- Local memory and correction: Missed terms can be corrected and remembered locally for cross-paper memory; corrections influence future annotations.
- Local environment requirements: Python 3.11+, Ollama, and Git; runs via a local UI at http://localhost:8503. No API key required for core features.
- Typical model setup (via Ollama): qwen3.5:4b for equation reading/math explanations; qwen2.5:7b for concept synthesis, Paper Chat, and judging; qwen2.5:3b as a tighter-hits fallback.
- Configuration and keys: Optional on-demand web-enabled research via Tavily and Semantic Scholar metadata; alternative backends via OpenAI; Langfuse for evaluation tracing when enabled.
- Workflow steps: Upload PDF, inspect annotated terms/equations, provide corrections, use Paper Chat in various modes (Fast/Deep/Web/Explore), and rely on a built-in human-aligned judging rubric (grounding, symbol coverage, LaTeX fidelity).

If you’re specifically looking for an arXiv/ML paper reader that runs locally with Ollama and supports equation walkthroughs, this project fits that niche, offering local-first annotation, equation walkthroughs, and a modular “specialist” Paper Chat workflow.

**nikhil-sarin/NSArxivApp**: NSArxivApp is a full-stack, locally-first tool to discover, summarize, and relate ArXiv papers. It emphasizes a private knowledge base with semantic search, visual connections, and AI-driven reading aids, all configurable and runnable on your machine.

Key capabilities that address your query:
- Local/private workflow: Persistent library stored under data/, with offline access and reloading on restart.
- Local-first LLM options: Multi-provider support via a single env var, including Ollama (local), Gemini, Anthropic, and OpenAI. Default is Ollama.
- Local summarization and reading aids: Auto-summarization of papers and detailed guided reading reports, plus a “Chat with paper” feature where the LLM reads the PDF and answers in-context.
- Semantic search and knowledge graph: Vector-based search using sentence transformers; visual knowledge graph of paper connections by category and authors.
- Easy setup for Ollama: Clear .env configuration (SUMMARIZER_PROVIDER=ollama, OLLAMA_MODEL, OLLAMA_HOST) and commands to install/start Ollama and pull a model.
- Automated fetching: Scheduled daily searches or new-submission fetches via cron or launchd.
- Tech stack and components: Python-based backend with modules for ArXiv API, PDF extraction, vector DB (ChromaDB), NetworkX knowledge graph, Streamlit frontend, and a CLI fetch_job for scheduling.

What to expect if you’re aiming to run locally with Ollama:
- Requirements: Python 3.10+, 8–16 GB RAM, ~5 GB storage for local models and PDFs.
- Steps: Install Ollama, pull a model (gemma4:latest), run Ollama server, configure .env, and start the Streamlit UI.
- Features to leverage: Search by keywords/categories/date, view/save papers in Library, regenerate summaries, generate ArXivSelaa-style detailed reports, and chat with papers for in-context Q&A.

If you want a quick start for ML-focused reading on your machine, this project appears to fit well, with strong emphasis on privacy, local inference (via Ollama), and robust paper-centric workflows.
